section.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About Awake Craniotomy
section.intro: Awake craniotomy is a specialised brain surgery performed while the patient is conscious for part of the procedure, used mainly to protect speech, movement, and other vital functions. These answers explain what it involves, who may need it, and how international patients can find experienced centers.

items.a: An awake craniotomy is a brain surgery in which the patient is kept awake and responsive during the critical part of the operation. Surgeons temporarily wake the patient so they can speak, move, or follow commands while the tumour or abnormal tissue is removed. This real-time feedback helps protect areas that control language, movement, and vision. The scalp is numbed, so patients generally feel pressure rather than pain.

items.q: Why is a patient kept awake during brain surgery?
items.a: Patients are kept awake so surgeons can map and protect critical brain functions in real time. When a tumour sits near regions controlling speech, movement, or sensation, the team asks the patient to talk, count, name pictures, or move a limb while operating. If a response changes, the surgeon adjusts immediately. This approach may help remove more tumour while lowering the risk of permanent deficits, though outcomes vary by individual case.

An awake craniotomy is generally not painful because the brain itself has no pain receptors. The scalp, skull, and surrounding tissues are numbed with local anaesthetic, and sedation is used during opening and closing. Patients may feel pressure, vibration, or hear sounds but usually do not feel sharp pain. Anaesthesia teams monitor comfort closely throughout. Any discomfort should be discussed in advance so expectations and the sedation plan are clear.

items.q: What is brain mapping during awake surgery?
items.a: Brain mapping is a technique used during awake surgery to identify which areas control speech, movement, and other functions. The surgeon applies gentle electrical stimulation to small regions of the brain while the patient performs tasks like talking or moving a hand. Areas that produce a response are marked and preserved. This functional map guides how much tissue can be safely removed and is a key reason awake surgery is chosen for certain tumours.

An awake craniotomy may be considered when a brain tumour or lesion lies near regions controlling speech, movement, or other essential functions. It is often used for gliomas, tumours in or close to the language and motor areas, and some epilepsy surgeries. Suitability depends on tumour location, type, the patient's ability to cooperate, and overall health. The final decision is made by a neurosurgical team after imaging and detailed assessment.

items.q: Who is not a good candidate for awake craniotomy?
items.a: Awake craniotomy may not be suitable for patients who cannot stay calm and cooperative during surgery. This can include young children, people with significant confusion, severe anxiety, uncontrolled seizures, difficulty following instructions, or certain airway and medical conditions. In these situations, surgery under general anaesthesia with other monitoring methods may be preferred. Candidacy is assessed individually by the neurosurgeon and anaesthesia team, and preferences should be discussed openly beforehand.

items.q: How is an awake craniotomy performed?
items.a: An awake craniotomy is performed in stages combining sedation and wakefulness. The patient is sedated while the scalp is numbed and a section of skull is opened. They are then gently woken so the surgeon can map the brain and remove the tumour while checking speech and movement. Once the critical work is done, sedation is deepened again to close the site. The whole process is guided by imaging and continuous monitoring.

items.q: What are the risks or side effects of awake craniotomy?
items.a: Awake craniotomy carries risks similar to other brain surgery, including bleeding, infection, swelling, seizures, and temporary or lasting neurological changes such as speech or movement difficulty. Some patients feel anxiety, fatigue, or nausea during the procedure. Mapping is designed to reduce the chance of permanent deficits but cannot eliminate all risk. The specific risks depend on tumour location and health, and should be reviewed carefully with the treating surgical team.

items.q: How long does an awake craniotomy take and what is recovery like?
items.a: An awake craniotomy usually takes several hours, though the exact time depends on tumour size, location, and complexity. Many patients stay in hospital for a few days, sometimes with time in intensive care for monitoring. Early recovery may involve fatigue, headache, or temporary speech or movement changes that often improve with rehabilitation. Full recovery varies widely between individuals, and the surgical team provides a personalised timeline and follow-up plan.

items.q: How much does an awake craniotomy cost?
items.a: The cost of an awake craniotomy varies widely depending on the country, hospital, surgeon, imaging, hospital stay, and any complications. It is generally lower in countries like India compared with the United States or parts of Europe, but figures should be treated as estimates only. Final cost depends on diagnosis, tumour complexity, tests, intensive care needs, and length of stay. A detailed hospital quotation is the most reliable way to plan.

Awake craniotomy is offered in many countries with established neurosurgery programmes, including India, the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Singapore, and others. It requires specialised neurosurgeons, neuro-anaesthesia, brain mapping technology, and an experienced team, so it is usually performed at larger tertiary or academic hospitals. Availability at any specific center should be confirmed directly, along with the surgeon's experience with the patient's particular tumour type and location.

items.q: Is awake craniotomy available in India?
items.a: Awake craniotomy is available in India at several major neurosurgery centers with experienced brain tumour teams. These hospitals often have advanced imaging, intraoperative brain mapping, and neuro-anaesthesia support needed for the procedure. Many international patients consider India for its combination of specialist expertise and comparatively lower costs. Availability, surgeon experience, and suitability for an individual case should always be confirmed with the specific hospital before making travel or treatment plans.

items.q: What kind of hospital or center performs awake craniotomy?
items.a: Awake craniotomy is performed at specialised neurosurgery centers with a dedicated brain tumour or neuro-oncology team. These centers typically offer advanced MRI, intraoperative brain mapping, neuro-anaesthesia, neuropsychology support, and intensive care. Surgeon and team experience with awake procedures matters greatly for safety and results. When choosing a center, it is reasonable to ask about case volume, technology available, and outcomes for tumours similar to the patient's own.

items.q: How does awake craniotomy compare with surgery under general anaesthesia?
items.a: Awake craniotomy allows real-time testing of speech and movement, which surgery under full general anaesthesia cannot provide in the same way. For tumours near critical brain areas, this may help surgeons remove more tissue while protecting function. However, general anaesthesia remains appropriate for many tumours and for patients who cannot tolerate being awake. The best approach depends on tumour location, patient factors, and should be decided with the neurosurgical team.

items.q: Are there clinical trials involving awake craniotomy?
items.a: Clinical trials involving awake craniotomy exist, often studying brain mapping techniques, imaging methods, or combined treatments for gliomas and other tumours. Participation does not guarantee benefit, and eligibility is decided only after medical record review and investigator assessment. Trials usually have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria based on tumour type, prior treatment, and health. Patients interested in research options should discuss them with their neuro-oncology team and review trial details carefully.

items.q: What technologies improve the safety of awake craniotomy?
items.a: Several technologies may improve the safety of awake craniotomy, including functional MRI, diffusion tensor imaging to map nerve pathways, intraoperative navigation, and direct electrical brain stimulation. Some centers use intraoperative MRI or ultrasound to check tumour removal in real time. These tools support the surgical team but do not replace their judgement. Access to specific technologies varies by hospital and should be confirmed when comparing centers for a particular case.

items.q: How can international patients access awake craniotomy abroad?
items.a: International patients can access awake craniotomy by first sharing their MRI, pathology, and medical history with a chosen center for review. Access depends on hospital acceptance, medical assessment, travel fitness, and visa approval, none of which can be guaranteed in advance. It helps to obtain a written cost estimate and a second opinion before travelling. Planning should also cover a companion, post-surgery stay, rehabilitation, and follow-up care after returning home.

items.q: What reports are needed to plan an awake craniotomy?
items.a: To plan an awake craniotomy, doctors usually need recent brain MRI scans, any prior imaging, pathology or biopsy reports if available, and a summary of the patient's medical history and current medications. Details of previous surgeries, seizures, and neurological symptoms are also important. Complete, good-quality reports help the neurosurgical team assess suitability and give an accurate opinion. The treating center may request additional tests before confirming a plan or cost estimate.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with awake craniotomy?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant neurosurgery specialists or centers, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. It supports patients in comparing experienced brain tumour centers and preparing for consultations. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified neurosurgical and oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, tumour location, imaging, previous treatment, and overall health, not by CancerFax.
